content.narrative_summary: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC) is defined by predominant right ventricular dilatation and/or dysfunction with histological involvement and/or electrocardiographic abnormalities per published criteria. Consensus criteria include RV dysfunction (global or regional), histological fibrofatty replacement of cardiomyocytes, ECG anomalies, ventricular arrhythmias of RV origin, and familial disease or pathogenic variants in desmosomal protein genes. The clinical paradigm has since broadened to include concealed/subclinical phenotypes, biventricular or left‐dominant disease (often termed ALVC), as well as other descriptors such as arrhythmogenic dilated cardiomyopathy. The 2010 Task Force criteria remain applicable, and predominant LV involvement may also occur within the same family.

section_headings: 3.3. Other traits and syndromes associated with cardiomyopathy phenotypes
content.narrative_summary: Restrictive cardiomyopathy is defined by restrictive left and/or right ventricular pathophysiology with normal or reduced diastolic and systolic volumes and normal wall thickness, commonly presenting as biatrial enlargement; left ventricular systolic function can be preserved initially but may evolve to a hypokinetic-dilated phase. Restrictive physiology may also occur in end-stage hypertrophic or dilated cardiomyopathies or due to endocardial pathology. Left ventricular hypertrabeculation (formerly LV non-compaction) describes a ventricular phenotype with prominent trabeculae and deep recesses, often familial and associated with variants in sarcomere, Z-disc, cytoskeleton, and nuclear envelope genes; it may also be transient or acquired, and is recommended to be termed ‘hypertrabeculation’ rather than a distinct cardiomyopathy. Takotsubo syndrome is a transient regional systolic dysfunction of the LV apex/mid-ventricle occurring in the absence of coronary disease, often precipitated by stress in post-menopausal women, with characteristic ECG changes and elevated catecholamines; function usually normalizes over days to weeks, and it is not classified as a cardiomyopathy by the Task Force. Epidemiology of cardiomyopathies varies globally with genetic influences and diagnostic criteria affecting prevalence estimates; true population prevalence is limited by study methods, with idiopathic DCM potentially tenfold higher in systematic studies. No specific data exist for non-dilated LVNC phenotype, and metrics for major cardiomyopathies are summarized in Table 4.

content.narrative_summary: Section 6.1 outlines how patients with cardiomyopathy present via primary, secondary, or tertiary pathways—triggered by symptoms, incidental findings, or genotype-first screening—and emphasizes a systematic cardiomyopathy-oriented evaluation across care settings. content.title: 6.6. Laboratory tests
content.narrative_summary: Section 6.6 describes the role of routine and additional laboratory tests in detecting extracardiac conditions (e.g. thyroid disease, renal dysfunction, diabetes) and assessing disease severity, aetiology, and secondary organ dysfunction in patients with suspected or confirmed cardiomyopathy. Section 6.7.1 outlines general principles of non-invasive multimodality imaging (ultrasound, CMR, CT, PET, scintigraphy), emphasizing yield, costs, limitations, patient safety, and the use of standardized algorithms. Section 6.7.2 summarizes the utility of transthoracic and advanced echocardiographic techniques (strain imaging, 3D echo, contrast echo, stress echo) for diagnosis, assessment of ventricular function, dynamic obstruction, and guiding management, including use of z-scores for paediatric measurements.

content.narrative_summary: Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) offers non-invasive tissue characterization important for diagnosing NDLVC, ARVC, myocarditis, amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, and iron overload. Initial evaluation should include cine imaging sequences, T2-weighted sequences, T1 mapping, and late gadolinium enhancement, with T2* mapping when haemochromatosis is suspected. Findings guide diagnosis and therapy and should be integrated with genetic and clinical data by experienced operators. Serial CMR every 2–5 years assists in monitoring disease progression and therapy efficacy. Special considerations include recent techniques allowing scans without general anaesthesia, evaluating risk–benefit in young children, managing artefacts from implantable devices, and protocols to reduce non-interpretable studies. Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis is a rare complication of first-generation linear gadolinium chelates.

content.title: 6.8 Genetic testing and counselling
content.narrative_summary: This section outlines the genetic architecture of cardiomyopathies, noting diverse inheritance patterns (autosomal dominant, recessive, X-linked, mitochondrial) and marked allelic heterogeneity. It describes incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity of pathogenic variants, non-Mendelian modifiers (eg, hypertension in HCM, exercise in ARVC), and the role of common small‐effect variants alongside rare Mendelian variants, spanning a continuum from monogenic to polygenic susceptibility. The text then discusses clinical genetic testing: focusing first on genes robustly associated with the presenting phenotype, extended analysis when initial testing is nondiagnostic, and the use of confirmatory, predictive, and cascade testing in relatives. It emphasizes genetic counselling to clarify variant pathogenicity, interpretation of uncertain variants, and consideration of secondary findings and opportunistic screening only when the balance of benefits and harms is established.

content.title: 6.10.3 Management of atrial arrhythmias
content.narrative_summary: This section discusses atrial fibrillation (AF) in cardiomyopathy patients, noting its prevalence and associated risks of stroke, heart failure, and death. Data from the EURObservational Research Programme show AF prevalence of ~28% at baseline, rising to ~31% on follow-up, with a registry incidence of ~3% per year. Integrated, structured AF management (ABC approach) is recommended, though evidence in cardiomyopathy is limited (~5–6%). The RACE 3 trial demonstrated that a structured care pathway reduced AF burden and rehospitalization. Anticoagulation is emphasized across cardiomyopathy subtypes due to elevated thromboembolic risk, with DOACs preferred over VKAs in AF without mechanical valves. Rate control should be considered in all cardiomyopathy patients with AF; beta-blockers are first line, with digoxin as an alternative for those intolerant of beta-blockers.

rows.recommendation: Following cascade genetic testing, clinical evaluation using a multiparametric approach that includes ECG and cardiac imaging and long-term follow-up is recommended in first-degree relatives who have the same disease-causing variant as the proband.

It is recommended that when no P/LP variant is identified in the proband or genetic testing is not performed, an initial clinical evaluation using a multiparametric approach that includes ECG and cardiac imaging is performed in first-degree relatives.

When no P/LP variant is identified in the proband or genetic testing is not performed, regular, long-term clinical evaluation using a multiparametric approach that includes ECG and cardiac imaging should be considered in first-degree relatives.

During cascade screening, where a first-degree relative has died, clinical evaluation of close relatives of the deceased individual (i.e. second-degree relatives of the index patient) should be considered.

content.narrative_summary: This page discusses the delayed penetrance of cardiomyopathy in women by approximately 10 years compared with men, and recommends cardiac screening every 1–3 years (with ECG and ECHO) before age 60 and every 3–5 years thereafter for carriers of pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP) variants or those with familial disease. It notes that penetrance of similar variants identified outside this context may be lower, and the benefits and harms of screening remain under evaluation. In special considerations for family screening, it suggests that if an index patient and informative relatives show isolated cardiomyopathy, periodic surveillance may be terminated in first‐degree relatives over 50 years with normal cardiac investigations. It also advises individualized periodic evaluation when inheritance patterns differ from autosomal dominant, including potential discharge of heterozygous carriers of recessive forms and delayed evaluation in X‐linked heterozygotes.

section_headings: 7.1.4.1.3. Invasive treatment of left ventricular outflow tract (septal reduction therapy)
content.narrative_summary: This section notes that there are no data supporting invasive reduction of LVOTO in asymptomatic patients, though retrospective data link high LVOT gradients (even if minimally symptomatic) to increased long-term mortality compared to those with lower gradients. Delaying septal reduction therapy (SRT) beyond five years from first detection may worsen outcomes, whereas earlier intervention may reduce complications and improve prognosis. Invasive SRT should be considered for patients with LVOTO gradient ≥50 mmHg and severe symptoms (NYHA III–IV) or recurrent syncope despite maximally tolerated therapy; it may also be considered in patients with mild symptoms (NYHA II) refractory to medical therapy who have resting or provoked gradient ≥50 mmHg plus moderate-to-severe systolic anterior motion-related mitral regurgitation, atrial fibrillation, or significant left atrial dilation at expert centres. The most common surgical procedure is ventricular septal myectomy, creating a trough in the basal septum.

section_headings: 7.1.5. Sudden cardiac death prevention in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
content.narrative_summary: The section discusses the annual incidence of cardiovascular death in adults with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM), highlighting sudden cardiac death (SCD) rates and common arrhythmic events. figures_tables_algorithms.title: Major clinical features associated with an increased risk of sudden cardiac death
figures_tables_algorithms.summary:
Risk factors and associated comments:
- Age: increased SCD risk in younger HCM patients; some studies show significant associations; rare <6 years.
- NSVT: defined as ≥3 ventricular beats ≥120 b.p.m. lasting <30 s; predictor of SCD; low exercise association.
- Maximum LV wall thickness: greater severity measured by TTE correlates with SCD risk; wall thickness ≥30 mm highest risk.
- Family history of SCD at a young age: clinically significant when first-degree relative <40 years; de novo variants in pediatric HCM.
- Syncope: common but multifactorial; unexplained syncope within 6 months predicts higher SCD risk.
- Left atrial diameter: positive association with SCD and AF; measurement of LA size important.
- LV outflow tract obstruction: significant association with SCD risk; prognostic impact of provocable LVOTO unclear; conflicting childhood data.

content.narrative_summary: Section 7.1.5.1 defines LV apical aneurysms in HCM and reviews observational registry and meta-analysis data linking them to monomorphic VT and increased SCD risk; recent guidelines include aneurysms as an independent risk factor but recommend individualized ICD decisions based on established risk factors rather than aneurysm presence alone. content.narrative_summary: This section discusses the limited prognostic value of sarcomeric genetic variants in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) for predicting sudden cardiac death (SCD). Although some studies suggest pathogenic variants may confer higher SCD risk, overall evidence is inconsistent, and the Task Force does not recommend using sarcomeric status alone to guide primary prevention ICD implantation in low or intermediate risk patients. There are no randomized data supporting antiarrhythmic drugs for SCD prevention; observational evidence suggests amiodarone may reduce SCD incidence, while disopyramide does not. Beta-blockers and amiodarone remain indicated for symptomatic device patients. The validated HCM Risk-SCD model (and pediatric adaptations such as HCM Risk-Kids and PRiMaCY) is recommended for risk estimation and shared decision-making rather than fixed thresholds. The Task Force emphasizes individualized decisions, acknowledges model limitations (e.g. not validated post-myectomy or in elite athletes, metabolic/infiltrative disease), and calls for enhanced patient decision aids.

figures_tables_algorithms.summary: Figure 16 summarizes the recommendations for primary prevention ICD implantation in HCM in each risk category. These take into account not only the absolute statistical risk, but also the age and general health of the patient, socioeconomic factors, and the psychological impact of therapy. The recommendations are meant to be sufficiently flexible to account for scenarios that are not encompassed by the HCM Risk-SCD or HCM Risk-Kids models. These models should not be used in elite athletes or in individuals with metabolic/infiltrative diseases (e.g. Anderson–Fabry disease) and syndromes (e.g. Noonan syndrome). The models do not use exercise-induced LV outflow tract gradients and have not been validated before and after myectomy. The HCM Risk-SCD model has been validated in one study of adult patients following ASA, and a recent study has suggested that severe LVH and residual LVOTO are associated with an increased risk of SCD following ASA, with a modest C-statistic of 0.68.

content.title: 7.2 Dilated cardiomyopathy
content.narrative_summary: This section defines dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) by left ventricular (LV) dilation and systolic dysfunction unexplained by loading conditions or coronary artery disease. For index cases, LV end-diastolic dimensions >2 z-scores above normal (or >58 mm in males, >52 mm in females) and LVEF <50% are criteria. In relatives, isolated LV dilation with preserved function plus a familial variant or family history suffices for familial DCM. The diagnostic work-up includes clinical/family history, ECG, Holter, imaging (CMR central), genetic testing, and other tests. Comprehensive transthoracic echocardiography, including advanced techniques (tissue Doppler, speckle tracking) and contrast when needed, is recommended for all DCM patients.

content.narrative_summary: Restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM) carries the worst prognosis among cardiomyopathy phenotypes, with high rates of early death or transplantation in children and a 5-year survival of ~50% in genetic adult RCM. Clinical indicators of poor outcome include heart failure symptoms, reduced LV function, atrial enlargement, syncope, ischaemia, and elevated pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR), prompting recommendations for serial catheterization and risk-based interventions. The section on syndromic and metabolic cardiomyopathies outlines that detailed genotype-phenotype guidance is provided elsewhere; here, only key aspects of Anderson–Fabry disease are summarized, including its enzyme deficiency basis, classic and non-classic phenotypes, diagnostic criteria (α-Gal A and lyso-Gb3 measurements, genetic testing), and multisystem clinical course requiring multidisciplinary monitoring.

Section 8.1.2 outlines how vigorous exercise may trigger sudden cardiac death in cardiomyopathy patients, historically leading to restrictive exercise recommendations. Section 8.1.3 describes emerging data supporting moderate exercise safety in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) with low-risk profiles. content.narrative_summary: Pregnancy and the post-partum period increase cardiovascular risk in women with cardiomyopathy. Counseling on contraception and assisted reproduction should consider thrombosis risk, especially in women with WHO class III disease or on anticoagulation. Pre-pregnancy, women with known cardiomyopathy should have multidisciplinary evaluation including ECG, echocardiography, and exercise testing, with discussion of transgenerational risk. During pregnancy, management should be by a specialist team (cardiologists, obstetricians, anaesthetists, and others as needed) with a delivery plan addressing induction, labour, delivery, and post-partum surveillance.

content.narrative_summary: Sections 8.2.2.3–8.2.2.6 outline management of pregnant women with cardiomyopathy. Timing and mode of delivery should be individualized based on cardiomyopathy type, ventricular function, NYHA class, arrhythmia and thrombo-embolic risk; vaginal delivery is preferred when feasible but caesarean section is advised for obstetric or severe cardiac indications. Post-partum haemodynamic changes necessitate monitoring for at least 24–48 hours, with attention to drug safety in breastfeeding. Pharmacological treatment mirrors non-pregnant regimens, avoiding known teratogens (e.g., ACE-Is, ARBs, renin inhibitors), initiating drugs as late as possible at the lowest effective dose; specific antiarrhythmics are listed by tolerance and safety, and beta-blockers require fetal growth monitoring. Anticoagulation during pregnancy includes VKAs with INR monitoring or LMWH substitution, with peri-delivery LMWH/UFH strategies guided by anti-Xa levels. Device therapy or catheter ablation should be considered pre-pregnancy in high-risk arrhythmias, with ICD implantation delayed until after fetal viability and radiation shielding. In HCM, most tolerate pregnancy well but require risk stratification by WHO class and gradient assessment, with anticoagulation for AF and delivery planning for LVOTO. ARVC appears to have low peripartum mortality. In DCM, pregnancy does not always accelerate disease but LMNA genotype-positive women have worse event-free survival; predictors of maternal mortality include NYHA III/IV and EF <40%, with further risk factors (text continues).

If pre-natal diagnostic testing is to be pursued by the family, it is recommended that this is performed early in pregnancy, to allow decisions regarding continuation or co-ordination of pregnancy to be made.

recommendation_tables.title: Index patients

recommendation_tables.title: Family members

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for cardiac transplantation in patients with cardiomyopathy

recommendation_tables.title: Anticoagulation

recommendation_tables.title: Control of symptoms and heart failure

rows.recommendation: Atrial fibrillation catheter ablation is recommended for rhythm control after one failed or intolerant class I or III AAD to improve symptoms of AF recurrences in patients with paroxysmal or persistent AF and cardiomyopathy.

Atrial fibrillation catheter ablation is recommended to reverse LV dysfunction in AF patients with cardiomyopathy when a tachycardia-induced component is highly probable, independent of their symptom status.

recommendation_tables.title: General recommendations

rows.recommendation: Implantation of a cardioverter defibrillator is only recommended in patients who have an expectation of good quality survival >1 year.

It is recommended that ICD implantation be guided by shared decision-making that: is evidence-based; considers a person’s individual preferences, beliefs, circumstances, and values; and ensures that the person understands the benefits, harm, and possible consequences of different treatment options.

It is recommended that prior to ICD implantation, patients are counselled on the risk of inappropriate shocks, implant complications, and the social, occupational, and driving implications of the device.
It is not recommended to implant an ICD in patients with incessant ventricular arrhythmias until the ventricular arrhythmia is controlled.

recommendation_tables.title: Primary prevention

rows.recommendation: Comprehensive SCD risk stratification is recommended in all cardiomyopathy patients who have not suffered a previous cardiac arrest/sustained ventricular arrhythmia at initial evaluation and at 1–2 year intervals, or whenever there is a change in clinical status.
The use of validated SCD algorithms/scores as aids to the shared decision-making when offering ICD implantation, where available is recommended in patients with HCM.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for routine follow-up of patients with cardiomyopathy

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that all clinically stable patients with cardiomyopathy undergo routine follow-up using a multiparametric approach that includes ECG and echocardiography every 1–2 years.
Clinical evaluation with ECG and multimodality imaging is recommended in patients with cardiomyopathy whenever there is a substantial or unexpected change in symptoms.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for family screening and follow-up evaluation of relatives

rows.recommendation: Following cascade genetic testing, clinical evaluation using a multiparametric approach that includes ECG and cardiac imaging and long-term follow-up is recommended in first-degree relatives who have the same disease-causing variant as the proband.

Following cascade genetic testing, it is recommended that first-degree relatives without a phenotype who do not have the same disease-causing variant as the proband are discharged from further follow-up but advised to seek re-assessment if they develop symptoms or when new clinically relevant data emerge in the family.

It is recommended that when no P/LP variant is identified in the proband or genetic testing is not performed, an initial clinical evaluation using a multiparametric approach that includes ECG and cardiac imaging is performed in first-degree relatives.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for psychological support in patients and family members with cardiomyopathies

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that psychological support by an appropriately trained health professional be offered to all individuals who have experienced the premature sudden cardiac death of a family member with cardiomyopathy.

It is recommended that psychological support by an appropriately trained health professional be offered to all individuals with an inherited cardiomyopathy who receive an implantable cardioverter defibrillator.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation for evaluation of left ventricular outflow tract obstruction

rows.recommendation: In all patients with HCM, at initial evaluation, transthoracic 2D and Doppler echocardiography are recommended, at rest and during Valsalva manoeuvre in the sitting and semi-supine positions—and then on standing if no gradient is provoked—to detect LVOTO.

In symptomatic patients with HCM and a resting or provoked peak instantaneous LV outflow tract gradient <50 mmHg, 2D and Doppler echocardiography during exercise in the standing, sitting (when possible), or semi-supine position are recommended to detect provokable LVOTO and exercise-induced mitral regurgitation.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for medical treatment of left ventricular outflow tract obstruction

rows.recommendation: Non-vasodilating beta-blockers, titrated to maximum tolerated dose, are recommended as first-line therapy to improve symptoms in patients with resting or provoked LVOTO.

Verapamil or diltiazem, titrated to maximum tolerated dose, are recommended to improve symptoms in symptomatic patients with resting or provoked LVOTO who are intolerant or have contraindications to beta-blockers.

Disopyramide, titrated to maximum tolerated dose, is recommended in addition to a beta-blocker (or, if this is not possible, with verapamil or diltiazem) to improve symptoms in patients with resting or provoked LVOTO.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for septal reduction therapy

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that SRT be performed by experienced operators working as part of a multidisciplinary team expert in the management of HCM.

SRT to improve symptoms is recommended in patients with a resting or maximum provoked LVOT gradient of ≥50 mmHg who are in NYHA/Ross functional class III–IV, despite maximum tolerated medical therapy.

Septal myectomy, rather than ASA, is recommended in children with an indication for SRT, as well as in adult patients with an indication for SRT and other lesions requiring surgical intervention (e.g. mitral valve abnormalities).

recommendation_tables.title: Secondary prevention

rows.recommendation: Implantation of an ICD is recommended in patients who have survived a cardiac arrest due to VT or VF, or who have spontaneous sustained VT with haemodynamic compromise.

content.narrative_summary: This page presents continuation of recommendation tables addressing contraception, inheritance risk counselling, delivery mode, medication review, and anticoagulation in women with cardiomyopathies; recommendations for peri-operative ECG monitoring and evaluation in cardiomyopathy patients undergoing non-cardiac surgery; and guidance on identification and management of cardiovascular risk factors in cardiomyopathy patients. It also includes footnotes listing abbreviations and administrative sections on supplementary data, data availability, and author information.

rows.recommendation: Counselling on safe and effective contraception is recommended in all women of fertile age and their partners.
Counselling on the risk of disease inheritance is recommended for all men and women before conception.

Vaginal delivery is recommended in most women with cardiomyopathies, unless there are obstetric indications for caesarean section, severe heart failure (EF <30% or NYHA class III–IV), or severe outflow tract obstructions, or in women presenting in labour on oral anticoagulants.
It is recommended that medication be carefully reviewed for safety in advance of pregnancy and adjusted according to tolerability in pregnancy.
Therapeutic anticoagulation with LMWH or VKAs according to the stage of pregnancy is recommended for patients with AF.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for non-cardiac surgery in patients with cardiomyopathy

rows.recommendation: Peri-operative ECG monitoring is recommended for all patients with cardiomyopathy undergoing surgery.

In patients with cardiomyopathy and suspected or known HF scheduled for intermediate or high-risk NCS, it is recommended to re-evaluate LV function with echocardiography (assessing LVOTO in HCM patients) and measurement of NT-proBNP/BNP levels, unless this has recently been performed.

It is recommended that cardiomyopathy patients with high-risk genotypes or associated factors for arrhythmic or heart failure complications or severe LVOTO be referred for additional specialized investigations to a cardiomyopathy unit before undergoing elective NCS.
In patients aged <65 years with a first-degree relative with a cardiomyopathy, it is recommended to perform an ECG and TTE before NCS, regardless of symptoms.
